1.sense: Seven things are sworn by in the first seven verses of this surah, the longest run of oaths at the head of anything in the Qur'an. The first is the sun, and specifically its duha, the stretch of morning when the light has climbed high enough to be full but has not yet turned hard.

notes.t: Duha is a named part of the day in Arabic, not a general word for brightness. It sits after sunrise and before the sun stands at its highest, and a whole prayer takes its name from it.
The Prophet ﷺ named this surah among the ones Muʿadh should have led his people with, after Muʿadh had kept them standing too long with a longer one.
The oaths run outward and then inward: sun, moon, day, night, sky, earth, and then a single self. The sequence narrows all the way down to one person, and that is where the surah puts its claim.

links.why: a whole surah opening on the same word for the morning light
the sun made a lamp and the moon a light in the same sentence

2.sense: The moon is sworn by at the moment it comes after the sun. Its light is borrowed and its position in the sentence is second, and the oath takes it at exactly that point rather than at the full moon.

notes.t: Tala means to follow, and it is the same verb behind tilawa, the recitation of a text. A reciter follows the words one after another the way the moon follows the sun, which is why the Qur'an uses one root for both.
What the following consists of is read two ways: the moon rising as the sun sets in the middle of the month, or the moon taking its light from the sun and so coming after it in that sense.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both the timing reading and the light reading

notes.t: The pronoun in talaha refers back to the sun, which in Arabic is grammatically feminine while the moon is masculine. The surah keeps every one of its fifteen verses ending on that same feminine ha.

links.why: the sun given as a shining thing and the moon as a derived light
neither is permitted to overtake the other

3.sense: Day is sworn by as the thing that shows the sun, rather than the other way round. The order is turned deliberately, so that time and the light in it are set beside each other instead of one being made to explain the other.

notes.t: Jalla is to polish something until it shows clearly. The same root gives the word for a bride being unveiled at her wedding, and for a matter becoming plain after being obscure.
The object of jallaha is disputed. Most exegetes take it as the sun, following the previous verses. Others read it as the earth or the world, which is not named anywhere in the sentence.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries both the sun and the unnamed world as the referent of the pronoun

notes.t: A neighbouring surah puts day and night in the same order with almost the same verbs, which is one reason the two are usually read as a pair.

links.why: by the day when it shows itself, two surahs later
He darkened its night and brought out its morning light

4.sense: Night is sworn by as an act of covering rather than as an absence. Ghisha is the verb for pulling a cloth over a thing, so darkness is described as something laid on top of light, not as what is left when light stops.

notes.t: The verb switches tense here. The two verses before used the past, talaha and jallaha, and this one uses the present, yaghshaha. Arabic uses that shift to make an action recurrent rather than finished.
The same root gives ghishawa, the covering laid over the eyes of those who will not see, and al-ghashiya, the event that comes over everything at the end.
A covering can be lifted, and the surah is building toward a verse about a soul buried out of sight. Night is the first thing in it that hides something without destroying it.

links.why: by the night when it covers, the identical verb opening the next surah but one
by the night as it closes in

5.sense: The sky and the building of it are sworn by together. The verb is the ordinary one for putting up a house, so the sky is presented as a structure with a builder and not as an expanse that happens to be there.

notes.t: The particle ma is normally used for things and man for persons, so its use here is discussed. Many read it as making a verbal noun, and the building of it; others read it as the One who built it, since ma can carry that in Arabic when the description matters more than the identity.
notes.src: az-Zamakhshari prefers the verbal noun reading; at-Tabari carries both

notes.t: Bana gives bina', a building, and the Qur'an calls the sky exactly that in one of its earliest arguments for worshipping the One who made it.
Three verses have sworn by light and time, things nobody handles. This one moves to construction, an act every listener in Mecca had watched being done by hand.

links.why: the earth a bed and the sky a building, in the same breath
We built the heaven with power and We are its expander

6.sense: The earth and the spreading of it. Taha is a rare verb, glossed by the lexicographers as driving a thing outward and away in every direction, and it does not occur anywhere else in the Qur'an.

notes.t: Taha appears once in the entire Qur'an, here. Its near twin daha, used of the earth in Surah An-Naziʿat, is also rare, and both carry outward extension rather than flattening.
Sky then earth, built then spread. Each of the two verses gives its half of the world a verb of workmanship, which keeps the oath from being an appeal to scenery.
The lexicographers explain taha with the image of pushing something out until it lies open in front of you, the way a rug is sent across a floor.

links.why: the earth spread out after that, with the sister verb
Allah made the earth for you a thing spread open

7.sense: The last of the seven oaths leaves the sky and the earth and comes down to a single self, and it is left indefinite. Not the soul, but a soul, which is any of them, and includes the one holding the page.

notes.t: Every previous oath took a definite noun: the sun, the moon, the day, the night, the sky, the earth. This one alone is indefinite, nafsin, and the narrowing from six named enormities to one unnamed person is the work of the whole opening.
Sawwa is to make even, balanced and complete. The Qur'an uses it for the forming of the human being, where it is followed immediately by the mention of proportion in the limbs.

The grammarians differ over where the answer to these oaths begins. Most take verse nine as the answer with its opening lam left out, since Arabic drops it when the statement is long; a few hold that the answer is omitted altogether.
notes.src: the grammarians of tafsir differ; the majority read verse nine as the answer with an elided lam

links.why: who created you, then proportioned you, then balanced you
then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit

8.sense: With the shaping came the knowledge of both directions. The verse does not say a rule book was handed over. It says the recognition of what breaks and what protects was put inside the self at the level where a person does not have to be taught.

notes.t: Ilham is knowledge placed into a self without instruction from outside. The root also gives iltiham, swallowing something whole, which is the physical picture underneath: it goes in without being chewed over.

Fujur comes from a verb meaning to split open, used of a dam giving way. Taqwa comes from wiqaya, a shield or a guard. So the pair is bursting out against holding in, and both are described as native to the same self.
The Prophet ﷺ asked for the second half of this verse directly: O Allah, give my soul its taqwa and purify it, for You are the best of those who purify it, You are its Guardian and its Master.

links.why: and We showed him the two elevations
We guided him to the road, whether grateful or ungrateful

9.sense: The answer to seven oaths is one short sentence about a person nobody can see. Everything sworn by was enormous, and what it was sworn over is what a single self quietly does with itself.

notes.t: Aflaha is from falah, which the lexicographers connect to splitting the ground open. The Arabic word for a ploughman, fallah, comes from the same root, and the picture is of breaking soil so that something can come up through it.
Zakka carries cleaning and growing at once. Zakah is a payment that takes from a pile and is described as increasing it, and the same verb is used here of what a person does to his own self.
The Qur'an states the same outcome in almost the same words in a surah nearby, and there it is placed after the remembrance of the name of the Lord.

links.why: he has succeeded who purified himself, said with the same verb
the counterweight, that none of you would ever be pure without His favour

10.sense: The other half, and the verb is not destroyed but hidden. The failure named here is not a self that was killed off. It is one that was pushed down out of sight and left there to shrink.

notes.t: The root is d-s-s, to slip something in or push it under. The Qur'an uses the same verb for a man burying his infant daughter in the dust to be rid of the shame of her, which is the image behind this one word.
Khaba is the failure of a hope rather than of a plan. It is what you say about a man who set out expecting something and came back with nothing in his hands.

Both verbs in verses nine and ten are done by the person to himself. Nobody purifies him and nobody buries him, and the surah spends seven oaths establishing who made the self before it says what the self does with itself.

links.why: the same root used of a child hidden in the ground
he has failed who carries wrongdoing, the same verb for failure

11.sense: The rule about the two souls is now given a worked case. A people denied, and the verse names the cause of the denial as their own habit of going past the limit, which puts the conduct first and the creed second.

notes.t: Taghwa is from tagha, to overflow a bound. The Qur'an uses the same verb for the flood water rising past everything that had held it, which is the physical sense the moral one is built on.
The bi in bitaghwaha is causal: they denied by reason of their transgression. The verse is not saying they overstepped because they denied, which is the order most people assume.

Thamud were a real people with rock-cut dwellings on the trade road north of Medina, which is why the Qur'an can use them as a case rather than a parable. Their name appears in the surah before this one with no story attached at all.

links.why: the same people named beside Pharaoh with the story withheld
the fuller telling, from Salih's arrival to the she-camel

12.sense: One man stands up out of the group. He is not called the strongest or the bravest of them, though he was reckoned that at the time. He is called the most wretched, which is the outcome given before the act.

notes.t: Inbaʿatha is the seventh verbal form, which in Arabic carries being roused or being set going. He got to his feet, and the grammar leaves room for the crowd that put him there.
The Prophet ﷺ referred to this verse in a sermon and described the man who rose as one of standing among his people, protected by his clan, not a marginal figure.
notes.src: Bukhari records it in his tafsir of this surah, from ʿAbdullah ibn Zamʿa

notes.t: Ashqa is the superlative of shaqi, wretched, the standing opposite of saʿid, fortunate. The Qur'an sorts people into those two on the Day, so the word carries the final verdict into the middle of the story.

links.why: they called their companion and he took the blade and hamstrung her
they hamstrung her and defied the command of their Lord

words.g: and her turn at the water

13.sense: Salih is not named here. He is called the messenger of Allah, and his warning is four words long: the camel of Allah, and her drink. What was at stake was a rota at a well.

notes.t: Naqatallahi stands in the accusative, which in Arabic signals a dropped verb of warning. The sense is beware the camel of Allah, not this is the camel of Allah. The grammar makes it a shout rather than a description.
Suqya is a turn at the water, not water in general. The Qur'an spells the arrangement out elsewhere: one day for her and one day for them, each on a known day.
Leaving the messenger unnamed keeps the emphasis on the office rather than the man. A people were not refusing Salih, they were refusing someone sent, and that is the description the verse chooses.

links.why: the watering rota stated exactly, a drink for her and a drink for you
this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign, so leave her to eat

14.sense: Four actions joined by fa, the particle that means each one followed the last with nothing in between. Denial, then the killing, then the crushing, then the levelling. The verse moves at the speed the event moved.

notes.t: ʿAqara is to cut the hamstring so the animal goes down, and then to finish it. One man rose in verse twelve and here the verb is plural, so the whole people are made to carry what one pair of hands did.

Damdama is a doubled root, the shape Arabic reserves for repeated or heavy sound and motion. The lexicographers gloss it as bringing destruction down over a thing until nothing stands proud of the ground.
Sawwaha is the same verb used in verse seven of a soul being proportioned. The one act of levelling makes a self and unmakes a town, and the surah uses the word both ways within eight verses.

links.why: the shaking seized them and morning found them face down in their homes
the same verb used to make rather than to flatten

15.sense: The surah ends on what does not happen afterwards. A ruler who levels a town has to think about the next town, the reprisal and the account of it. The last line says that consideration has no place here.

notes.t: ʿUqba is what comes behind, from ʿaqib, a heel. The word is the trailing consequence of an act, the thing that follows it home.

Who the verb belongs to is read two ways: He does not fear the aftermath, meaning Allah, or he did not fear it, meaning the man who hamstrung her. Most of the exegetes take the first, which is why the surah closes on the doer rather than the deed.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir carry both, with the majority reading it of Allah

notes.t: Fifteen verses end on the same feminine ending, and this is the last of them. The surah is one long rhyme that opens on a sunrise and closes on an empty valley.

links.why: He is not questioned about what He does, and they are questioned
the doer of whatever He intends, the same point made from the other side
